Odin in Godot

6 · Identity, recovery, and transport testing

3 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓
Persistent identitySavesHost migrationTransports: Steam and webTesting under latencyFurther guides

This post covers persistent identity, saves, cooperative host migration, Steam and web transports, and integration tests under latency. Each feature needs session configuration and game-specific recovery or deployment work.

Persistent identity#

ksave.token supplies a persistent reconnect token from an environment variable for tests or a file under user:// for ordinary play. An opt-in per-instance salt distinguishes clients in same-machine tests. Seats are keyed by token, so replacing a connection does not create a new player identity:

  • Crash and rejoin reclaims the retained seat, stats, and entities. For example, a returning player keeps seat 2 rather than receiving seat 5.
  • Kick and ban apply to the token identity across connections (session_kick(player, ban)).
  • A locked session (session_set_locked) still admits returning identities to their retained seats.

Tokens are hashed on the host and never relayed to other peers.

Saves#

ksave.save_write writes the authority's complete session snapshot together with save metadata and a game blob. That snapshot includes the roster, stats, and registered entities. It is distinct from a recipient's network snapshot, which may be filtered and need not contain enough state to resume authority.

Odin
ksave.save_write(&self.ses, &w, GAME_VERSION, my_campaign_blob)  // save
blob, err := ksave.resume(&self.ses, name, path, GAME_VERSION)   // load and resume

The session snapshot carries identity, stats, entities, and replicated fields. Use the game blob for other authority state, such as AI clocks and the wave director. Restore that state when resuming. Friends then rejoin the resumed run with their tokens, as they would after a dropped connection.

Host migration#

Backup snapshots stream to a designated client every few seconds. On host loss, that client rebinds as the server and resumes the session from the backup. Other peers reconnect with their tokens during the run. The integration test exercises this path by sending kill -9 to the host process.

Wire Ev_Backup_Target and Ev_Succession, provide the successor's address, and include game-specific authority state in backups. Recovery uses the last backup and retained identities so players can continue without creating a new lobby. Live migration supports the cooperative lane; it requires no installed simulation lane. Post 7 describes that limit.

Transports: Steam and web#

The native session can use ENet on localhost, a LAN, or a VPS. Godot's MultiplayerPeer abstraction lets the session use other transports. For Steam, create or join a lobby, install its peer, and invite players through the overlay. Replication and command code continue to use the session APIs. Browser exports use WebRTC and require the corresponding connection setup.

Testing under latency#

Multi-process integration tests exercise packet timing, latency, and differences between host and client behavior. Kit's game examples test these conditions by running the game and driving its exposed methods:

  • launch two or three real game processes headless, over real sockets, with 120ms injected latency;
  • a driver script plays each role through the game's own @(gd_method) surface (host, join, act, kill the host mid-run);
  • each process prints one-line facts (GOLF_CLAIM kind=1, GOLF_GEM_GONE kind=1), and the harness greps that every peer saw what it should, including that the observer's screen presented the effect, not just the actor's.

The addon ships the harness template (build/template/test/ + kit/testing); adapting it to a new game is a project-specific task. A passing latency test checks this scenario; also verify the export target, deployment, and failure cases your game supports.

Further guides#

  1. Getting Started covers the toolchain through moving a node, if you haven't already.
  2. Build a game in a day is the step-by-step recipe: lobby → entity → movement → verbs → combat → levels → save → migration → Steam.
  3. Read a finished game against it, such as examples/cavecrawl, and keep kit/ open as the per-package reference.
  4. Build and test each addition before adding the next feature.

These features use the tagged fields, validating commands, and presentation procedures from the earlier posts. Keep their ownership and timing rules explicit as you add identity, recovery, and transports to the game.
